lawyer:
Dr Rafiqur Rahman with MA Baqui, Advocates------ For the Petitioners. 
Md Khalilur Rahman with TM Shakil Hasan, Advocate------ For the Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Dhaka City Corporation and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Shamsur Rahman and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Earlier Rule was obtained by defendant Nos. 1 to 3 on behalf of the Dhaka City Corporation, in short, the DCC, upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and decree dated 24-5-05 passed by Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 393 of 2004, which reversed the judgment and decree dated 6-11-04 of the trial Court and decreed the suit as prayed for.

2. Later Rule was obtained by defendant No, 4 upon similar revision application against same judgment and decree of reversal. Defendant No.4 appears to be a multipurpose co-operative society of motor parts owners.

3. Opposite party No.1 as plaintiff on 27-11-02 instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 308 of 2002 against the petitioners and another for a decree of declaration that RS record of rights as prepared and finally published in the name of erstwhile DIT now added defendant No.5, RAJUK, in respect of the suit land measuring about 0.3480 acres of RS plot No. 9541 fully described in the schedule 'Kha' a part of schedule 'Ka' measuring about 0.6281 acre was wrong, illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the application of defendant No. 4 dated 13-10-02 submitted before defendant No.2 for lease of the suit land was illegal, ineffective and also not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff also prayed for perpetual injunction for restraining defendant Nos. 1 and 2 permanently from leasing out the suit land or any part thereof in favour of defendant No. 4 or any other third party and/or also for restraining them from interfering in any way with the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. The suit was then renumbered as aforesaid Title Suit No. 124 of 2003. By an order dated 2-4-03 RAJUK was added as defendant No.5.

4. Plaint case, in short, is that the land measuring about 0.6864 acre of plot No. 118 appertaining to CS khatian No. 13369 was originally owned and possessed by Indro Mohan and Rajkumar and Mukta Sundari in equal shares. Indro Mohan and Mukta Sundari died without any issue and leaving Rajkumar as their only heir and legal representative. Rajkumar was survived by two sons, namely, Radhagobinda and Pratap Chandra. By successive devolution, Radhagobinda and others became owners in possession of said land. They on 2-1-54 transferred said land to the plaintiff by way of a registered 'Patta' being No. 7441 and a registered sale deed being No. 7442 and delivered possession. Record of rights was accordingly prepared in the names of said recorded tenants and the plaintiff in SA khatian No. 2190 in plot No. 6163. Said land was also recorded as holding No. 47 Lal Chan Mokim Lane in the office of defendant No. 4, the DCC.

5. Then, on the requisition of the erstwhile DIT for making a road over the Dholaikhal in LA Case No. 37/1961-62 land measuring 0.3018 acre out of said 0.6864 acre was requisitioned.

6. The plaintiff originally received as compensation Taka 9,856 for said acquisition. Ultimately, 0.0583 acre out of the requisitioned land was used for the road. Land measuring about 0.2435 acre remained unused. The plaintiff amalgamated said unused land with his land into 0.6281 acre and filled with earth and constructed 62 semi-pucca shops. Said shops were comprised of a supermarket under the name and style "Shamsur Rahman Boro Market". The plaintiff kept two shops in his possession and let out others.

7. Then RAJUK decided to release the unused land and on the application of the plaintiff, the Ministry of Land by its memo dated 24-3-86 released 0.1482 acre of land in favour of the plaintiff and asked the DC, Dhaka to complete the process of release. When by an order dated 8-4-86 the plaintiff was asked to return Taka 5229.90 proportionate price of the released land out of the compensation received, the plaintiff on 8-4-86 deposited said amount by treasury 'Chalan'. Then, pursuant to the final order of release dated 19-4-86, the government handed over formal possession of said released land to the plaintiff. Meanwhile, in the revision survey, the plaintiff found that said land measuring about 0.3480 acre schedule 'Kha' part of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of erstwhile DIT and such record of rights had got no basis.

8. It is further stated that when some of the tenants defaulted in the payment of rents, the plaintiff had to institute suits for their eviction. Defaulting tenants then approached the DCC and claimed in collusion with the DCC depositing rents in the Sixth Court of Assistant Judge at Dhaka. Then, the DCC at the instigation of defaulted tenants on 27-6-02 most illegally asked the plaintiff to show cause as to why he should not be evicted from the suit land. The representation submitted on behalf of the plaintiff was not still disposed of by the DCC.

9. The tenants of the plaintiff then formed them into a society as defendant No.4 and made an application on 13-10-02 to the DCC for allotment. A server on behalf of the DCC came to the suit land on 6-11-02 for measurement. Then, the plaintiff came to know about the wrong record of rights in respect of 0.3480 acres of land in the name of erstwhile DIT. Hence, the suit.

10. Defendant Nos. 1 to 3 in one set and defendant No. 4 alone contested by filing two separate written statements.

11. Case of the defendant Nos. 1 to 3, in brief, is that land of schedule 'Kha' measuring about 0.3480 acre was acquired in the aforesaid LA Case for building of Dholaikhal Road. Then by a memo dated 5-6-82 the DIT transferred Dholaikhal and the adjacent land to the DCC. Being thus owner in possession, the DCC started development of the road, footpath, drain, etc, which was still pending. Said land was recorded in the name of the DCC. Such record of rights shows possession of the DCC.

12. It was further stated that the plaintiff got recorded 0.3292 acre in his name in the DP Khatian No. 5392 behind the back of the DCC. Against said record of rights, an appeal was filed and decided wrongly against the DCC. Then, an application was made for review which was fixed for hearing on 25-6-03. Against the review order, the petitioner moved this Division and got a stay in Writ Petition No. 4522 of 2003. By transfer from the DIT the DCC became owner of the suit land. The plaintiff has got no right or title in the suit land and the suit was therefore not maintainable.

13. Defendant No. 4 contended that after requisition of the land of CS plot No. 118 by the DIT in the aforesaid case of 0.6281 acres remained unused. The members of defendant No.4, 'Samity' raised on their own cost 62 shops on said unused land and started business of old iron. When the plaintiff claimed to be owner of the suit land, defendant No. 4 and its members entered into monthly lease agreement with him due to ignorance and started paying rents thinking the plaintiff was the real owner of the land. On 25-4-02, the DCC demanded ownership of the suit shops. When the matter was brought to the notice of the plaintiff, he could not do anything. Then, people of DCC on 8-2-02 came to the land and disclosed that they would be evicted unless they started paying rents to the DCC. When it was informed to the plaintiff, he could not take any step. On 27-6-02 the DCC issued notice upon the members of defendant No. 4 for eviction. Being thus compelled, they took shelter of the Court and started depositing rents in the Court. Having learnt that the DCC was the owner of the suit land, they on 13-10-02 applied for allotment. The plaintiff is not entitled to any relief as the DCC was the owner of the suit land.

14. On the party pleadings, the trial Court settled five issues including,

(1) whether there was any cause of action for the suit?;

(2) Whether the suit is barred by limitation?; and

(3) Whether the plaintiff has got right, title, possession or interest in the suit land?

15. In support of his case, the plaintiff examined three witnesses including himself while defendants examined two witnesses for their each set. Papers and documents adduced by the plaintiff were marked Exhibits 1 to 14 and those of the defendants were marked as Exhibit 'Ka to Ka(4)".

16. On the evidence oral and documentary on the record, the trial Court was of the view that seeking declaration in respect of the wrong record of rights without praying for declaration of title in the suit land was not sufficient and upon such view, it dismissed the suit as not maintainable.

17. On appeal therefrom at the instance of the plaintiff, the appellate Court on the other hand on the evidence both oral and documentary on record found 0.2435 acre of land was finally released and the plaintiff returned the money as was required for such release of the unused land. It found possession of the plaintiff in the suit land which was admitted by defendant No. 4. It also found RS Khatian was wrongly recorded in the name of defendant No.5.

18. Upon such views, the appellate Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit as prayed for by impugned judgment and decree.

19. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, learned Senior Advocate appearing in the earlier Rule for and on behalf of the DCC, submitted that in view of transfer of the suit land to the DCC vide Exhibit 'Ka(2)', the DCC since possessed the suit land and the trial Court was also of the view that development work on behalf of the DCC was going on in the suit land. In such view of the matter, the appellate Court was wrong in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissing the suit.

20. He submitted that in the absence of a relief sought for declaration of title in the suit land as was found by the trial Court, the plaintiff was not entitled to a mere decree for declaration that RS record of rights as prepared and published was wrong.

21. Mr Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahammad, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of defendant No.4 in the later Rule, somehow adopted the submissions of Mr Rafiqur Rahman and submitted that the suit as framed was barred by limitation after acquisition and the Court of appeal below therefore fell in serious error in decreeing such time barred suit.

22. He also submitted that in view of the findings of the trial Court that development works at the instance of the DCC were going on over the suit land, the suit for perpetual injunction was not maintainable.

23. He also submitted that the trial Court was justified in dismissing the suit for want of declaration of title.

24. Lastly, he submitted that after requisition and acquisition, the plaintiff lost all right or interest in the suit land and the appellate Court committed serious error without notice of such legal consequence, which resulted in failure of justice. In support, he cited Bangladesh vs Samodra Narayan Mohajan and another 2006 BLD (AD) 145 =.11 BLC (AD) 226.

25. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party in both the Rules however, submitted that the acquisition case was not yet completed and the acquisition process was not yet final After release of the schedule 'Kha' land, the plaintiff possessed the entire suit land through tenants and two shops through his sons.

26. He submitted that the Court of appeal below rightly decreed the suit in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record and such decree does not call for any interference.

27. He submitted that when the plaintiff was admittedly owner in possession of the entire suit land and after release of schedule 'Kha' land, the plaintiff was not required to seek declaration of title and the suit instituted for declaration that the RS record of rights as prepared and published Was wrong was maintainable in law. In support, he cited Sarashijaksha Chatterjee and others vs Karpor Kamini Devi and others. AIR 1937 Calcutta 745.

28. Lastly, he submitted that if the Court found that the plaintiff was entitled to a relief on the case made out and proved but was not prayed for, the Court under Order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure can always grant such relief. In support, he cited S Sibtain Fazli vs Messrs Star Film Distributors 14 DLR 307; Kayemat Ali Sakidar and others vs Jainuddin Talukder, 14 DLR 657 and Commander (Retd) AA Chowdhury vs AKM Imam Hossain and others, 49 DLR 23.

29. I have perused the record.

30. Only issue facing me is, as to whether the Court of appeal below was justified in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court and in decreeing the suit in its entirety as prayed for.

31. The facts which do not admit of any controversy are, that the plaintiff was owner in possession of entire 0.6864 acre of land. In LA Case No. 37/1961-62 land measuring about 0.3018 acre out of said 0.6864 acre was required for construction of Dholaikhal Road at the requisition of the then DIT. Out of the requisitioned land 0.0583 acre only was used and 0.2435 acre of land remained unused.

32. It is the case of the plaintiff that land measuring about 0.1482 acre out of said unused land was first released by the acquiring body, that is the government, vide memo dated 24-3-86. Then, the government released 0.953 acre. On being asked to deposit Taka 5229.00 as proportionate price of the released land measuring 0.2435 acre to the plaint, the plaintiff deposited on 8-4-86 by a treasury 'Chalan' said amount out of total compensation of Taka 9856.00 received by him.

33. Amalgamated released land with his other land now measured about 0.6281 acre fully described in schedule 'Ka' and comprised of holding No. 47 Lal Chan Mokim Lane under the DCC. Plaintiff made 62 shops and let them out to different tenants excepting two shops, which his sons were carrying 011 business in.

34. Further case of the plaintiff was that the land of schedule 'Kha' measuring 0.3480 was recorded wrongly in the name of DIT in the revision survey in RS khatian No.6, which had no basis. In support of such case, he adduced evidence both oral and documentary.

35. Trial Court found that 0.3018 acre out of the land of the plaintiff was acquired in aforesaid acquisition proceeding. Out of said acquired land, 0.0583 acre was used. In view of Exhibits 8, 8(ka), 10 and 14 land measuring about 0.1482 acre seemed to have been released and formal possession was delivered to the plaintiff. But though rest 0.953 acre was claimed to have been released but in support of such release no separate order was submitted. By Exhibit 14, the plaintiff deposited the money price of released land as was asked to.

36. It was also the view of the trial Court that RS khatian might have been prepared in 1969/70 to 1972/73 and the plaintiff got release of the land in 1986. So, there was no occasion for recording the land in the name of the plaintiff. Such record of rights cast a doubt over the title of plaintiff and the declaration sought for in respect of the wrong record of rights was not sufficient in the absence of a declaration of title.

37. With regard to possession, the trial Court found that defendant No.4 paid rents to the plaintiff as landlord, which they did not deny. Plaintiff adduced exhibits 4 to 6 series to evidence lease agreements with the tenants, payment of rents and taxes. Existence of shops in the suit land was also admitted. Shop owners never paid rent to the DCC as landlord. There was no proof that the DCC built the shops and/or the tenants were under the DCC.

38. The trial Court further found that the acquisition was not yet final. The suit was therefore, not barred by limitation.

39. The trial Court dismissed the suit as not maintainable on the view that after acquisition, there were development works and the record of rights was prepared in the name of DCC. I find no justification for such observation. The finding of the trial Court that there were development works on the suit land has got no basis since it is admitted that the suit land is now occupied by shops and there cannot be thought of and development works by the DCC in the shops,

40. The Court of appeal below however, on consideration of Exhibits 7, 8/Ka, 9 and 10 found in clear terms that out of required 0.3018 acre, 0.0583 acre was used by the requiring body in building footpath and road and the government de-requisitioned in two installments 0.2435 acre and received back proportionate price of said released land.

41. The fact that the plaintiff amalgamated derequisitioned land with his other land and built a market there and let out the shops to the tenants was proved and admitted, Consequently, the plaintiff had got title and possession in the entire suit land and preparation and publication of RS record of rights in the name of RAJUK was wrong, illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff.

42. It also found that no notice under sub-section 7 of section 5 of the Emergency (Requisition) of Property Act, 1948 was published by the government. Upon such view, it reversed the finding of the trial Court that the suit without declaration of title was not maintainable.

43. Neither the acquiring body, the government nor the requiring body the erstwhile DIT now RAJUK appear in and contest the suit. Section 8 of the Emergency (Requisition) of Property Act, 1948, empowers the Deputy Commissioner only to release unused land. Claim of the DCC that it got possession of said unused land of 0.2435 acre from the DIT vide memo dated 3-6-82 and thereby became owner of said land is nothing but a hoax and was correctly rejected by the Court of appeal below. The trial Court could not go that far to accept the case of the DCC.

44. Members of defendant No.4, who having admitted to be tenants of the plaintiff and paid rents to him, would not be allowed to change their standing and/or disowning their landlord before surrender of possession of their respective premises. On such view of the legal position of the tenants, submissions of Mr Khondakar Mahbubuddin have got no substance.

45. On the aforesaid findings, there is little difficulty to hold that the plaintiff became owner in possession of 0.3480 acre as described in schedule 'Kha'. Said land was finally recorded and published in the name of the erstwhile DIT. Such record has got no basis. Decree passed by the Court of appeal below declaring such record of rights prepared in respect of said 0.3480 acre in plot No. 9541 in the name of the DIT wrong, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff is well justified in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record.

46. The trial Court however tried to find that when the record of rights was prepared the plaintiff did not get back possession of said unused land of 0.2480 acre. Such record of rights cast a cloud over the title of the plaintiff Upon such view, it finally found that the suit was not maintainable without declaration of title.

<u>47. Such view of the trial Court was reversed rightly by the appellate Court. Because, the decision of the trial Court is based on no authority. Earlier, wrong record of rights could be corrected by a mere application under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. In such proceeding, the aggrieved party was never required to establish title to get an order for correction of the record of rights. Reason is not far away to find. Record of rights does neither create nor destroy title. It is mere a record of physical possession at the time when it is prepared.</u>

48. A suit for declaration that the record of rights is wrong and for direction for correction of such record of rights falls under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. I find support from an old judgment of MC Ghosh, J in 1937 AIR Cal 745,

"Now in this case the plaintiffs asked for a declaration that the Record of Rights was wrong and they prayed that the said record might be corrected. The suit was therefore maintainable and the learned Judge was wrong to hold that it did not come under section 42."

49. The Court of appeal below decreed the suit that the record of rights as prepared in Khatian No. 06 in respect of 0.3480 acre of schedule 'Kha' in the name of DIT (RAJUK) was illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff as prayed for. I find such declaration was not sufficient, effective and complete relief. Because, the record of rights would not be corrected even after such declaration and continue to remain as before, with at best a copy of the decree attached with the relevant page.

50. It occasioned no doubt, for the omission in the prayer for correction of the record of rights in the name of the plaintiff. What can be done if the art of pleadings does not improve even over a century in this part of the civil law world But a litigant cannot be denied the relief which he is entitled to in law.

<u>51. Order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure in such case empowers the Court to give relief to the plaintiff as he is found entitled to but omit to pray. Otherwise, the plaintiff would be driven back to seek another declaration and/or correction of the record of rights in another suit which would not only cost the plaintiff but also consume valuable time of the Court.</u>

52. The question was settled long before by Mr Ali, J in 14 DLR 657. Let me quote him:

"There is no doubt that the plaintiff in his plaint might ask for an alternative relief, that is, he might ask that he might be given a declaration of his under raiyati right in the disputed lands under the defendants 1 and 2. But his omission can hardly be a sufficient justification for driving the parties to a separate suit for determination of the question determined in the present suit."

53. In 14 DLR 307 a Division Bench also took the view:

"It is always open to a Court to give a plaintiff such general or other relief as it deems just to the same extent as it had been asked for provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond that can be compensated for in costs.

54. Relying upon 14 DLR 307 a Division Bench in 49 DLR 23 took the view:

"The Code permits the grant of such general or other relief as the plaintiff is entitled to get upon the evidence even if the plaint does not contain a prayer for the relief"

55. On the other hand, the decree of the appellate Court declaring the application of defendant No.4 dated 13-10-02 submitted before defendant No.2 for lease illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff appears to be misconceived. Right of access to any authority, constitutional or statutory, is basic to a citizen of any jurisdiction. Such right to approach any such authority either by writing or otherwise cannot be denied. Only when an action is taken or omission occurred upon .such application or prayer that injures anyone the person feels aggrieved may have a cause of action against such action or omission. Such declaration therefore must be denied.

56. For foregoing reasons, ultimate decision of the appellate Court below does not suffer from any illegality or irregularity, which occasioned no failure of justice.

57. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost. The cost is assessed at Taka five thousand.

58. The suit is accordingly decreed declaring the record of rights as prepared and finally published vide Exhibit 11/Ka in respect of land measuring about 3480 described in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint in the name of the then DIT and now RAJUK in RS Khatian No. 6 is wrong, illegal, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiff. It is directed that the relevant record of rights must be corrected in the name of the plaintiff.

59. The defendants are accordingly, restrained by a decree of permanent injunction from disturbing and/or interfering with peaceful possession of the plaintiff in the suit land, in any way, as prayed for.

Send down the records, at once.

End.
